claim: Fireground commanders on hard, non-routine incidents mostly acted on the first recognised option: 127 of 156 decision points were recognition-type (about 81%), only 28 had more than one option identified, and 16 showed any relative evaluation. (Re-read in the DTIC report. Table 4 resolves as deliberated 18, constructed 11, analog 3 + prototype 124 = 127.)
agent_test: Build an incident-case set with expert first options; count how often the agent's first option is workable versus the best of N at equal tokens.

claim: The 81% figure is retrospective and inferred from interviews by one research group on hand-picked hard cases, and later reviews round it to 80-90%. It shows what experts reported, not that the first option was best.
agent_test: Do not use 81% as a prior in the scaffold; measure first-option hit rate directly.

claim: Recognition-primed decisions were reported in every one of the studies in a 32-study review of high-risk decision making that examined strategy (e.g. naval AEGIS officers: 95% of 77 actions recognitional vs 4% choosing among multiple options), though analytic strategies were also common when time pressure was lower and surgeons used RPD only about half the time; a sport review citing Macquet (2020) reports 60-81% of expert decisions as simple matches, 13-28% diagnosis and 3-24% evaluating a course of action.
agent_test: Tag agent trajectories as simple-match, diagnose or compare, and see which share the scaffold produces.
audit_note: Numbers match, but Reale et al. say RPD was found in every study that looked while analytic strategies were also common and surgeons used RPD only about half the time, and the sport 60-81% is Macquet (2020) cited second-hand; 'dominant across domains' is too strong.
claim_before_audit: Recognition-type decisions are the dominant reported strategy across domains: naval AEGIS officers 95% recognitional vs 4% multiple options; a 32-study review found RPD in every study that looked at strategy; sport reviews report 60-81% simple match.

claim: Surgeons in two interview studies reported recalling only one option in about half of the challenging cases they described (6 of 12; 11 of 24), the non-expert crews in the pumping-station fire mostly deliberated in group consultation, and one sport study (Basevitch et al.) found generating more options worked better when more time was available; these separate observations are consistent with, but do not test, a drop in single-option use for less routine tasks or less expert groups.
agent_test: Compare keep-first vs compare-N on items split by a typicality score at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers check (6 of 12, 11 of 24 one option; pumping fire mostly deliberated in consultation, non-expert crews), but the review does not show single-option use dropping with less routine tasks or less expert groups (two studies found time pressure had no effect; the comparison with other groups is the note's own inference), and only one sport study (Basevitch) ties more option generation to more time; a18 and b13 are the same review.
claim_before_audit: Reported use of single-option decisions drops when the task is less routine or the group is less expert: surgeons used one option in about half of cases (6 of 12; 11 of 24), the pumping-station fire was mostly deliberated in groups, and sport studies find more option generation when time allows.

claim: Experts and novices both used recognition, but experts built novel options and weighed future contingencies more (12 vs 12 fireground commanders; only 18% of decision points fit classical concurrent comparison); in sport, one study (Basevitch et al.) found generating more options worked better when more time was available, while another (Musculus) supported only less-is-more.
agent_test: Vary the option budget with available tokens and check whether best-of-N overtakes first-option at some threshold.
audit_note: Fireground numbers (12 vs 12, 18%, novel options, almost twice as likely to consider contingencies) match Klein & Calderwood 1990, but the sport half rests on a single study (Basevitch, via the review): Musculus found only less-is-more support and Raab & Johnson (equal option counts across expertise) say nothing about time.
claim_before_audit: Experts and novices both used recognition, but experts built novel options and weighed future contingencies more (12 vs 12 commanders; only 18% classical concurrent comparison), and in sport more time favours generating more options.

claim: Trust in the first recognised option is justified only in a high-validity environment with enough practice; confidence does not signal validity, and experts are skilled on some tasks and not others.
schema_part: G (confidence is not validity); validity check before keep-first
agent_test: Test whether the agent's confidence predicts first-option correctness on a regular domain versus a noisy one.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Statistical rules tie or beat expert clinical judgement in most studies reviewed, so recognition is weakest in low-validity domains.
schema_part: G: prefer explicit rule or check in low-validity tasks
agent_test: Compare first-option recognition with a simple rule on a low-validity forecasting set.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Mental simulation of the first option is the built-in check in RPD; the authors say recognition fails when the commander lacks experience or cannot simulate the option to find pitfalls. No controlled test of the simulation step alone was found. Gap search: LLM tests show a same-model review without outside feedback does not help (Huang 2024: GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 over two rounds) and approves most bad plans (Valmeekam 2023: 38 of 45 invalid plans passed), while simulating each candidate with a world model beat plain re-ranking (WebDreamer ablation). No ablation of simulation inside a keep-first agent exists.
agent_test: Ablate the simulate-the-option step in a keep-first agent at equal tokens.

claim: Mismatch of expectancies is the trigger to leave the first option: 3 of 156 points in the founding study were mismatch events; later work finds RPD phases are not strictly sequential; an agent model (R-CAST) with expectancy monitoring held up under time pressure.
agent_test: Give the agent an explicit expectancy list and test whether violations trigger a reroute earlier than plain generate-test.
audit_note: Minor: R-CAST result is for human-agent teams in a simulation (6 vs 6 teams, 9 speeds), attributing the gain to expectancy monitoring specifically is the authors' framing; the 16 s figure in a34 was not checked (8 s in the paper's text for the diagnose case) but is not used in the claim.

claim: Under time pressure, grandmasters did worse with rapid moves: 20 grandmasters made more and bigger blunders in blitz (blunder proportion t(19)=6.54, d=1.39; size d=0.96; worse for 18 of 20). This contradicts the strong reading that fast expert intuition is as good as slow thought.
schema_part: G: deliberation reserve for high-stakes steps
agent_test: Cap thinking tokens on a chess-puzzle or planning set and measure blunder rate versus an uncapped control.

claim: Classic pro-intuition chess evidence is thin or contested: Calderwood 1988 used 3 masters vs 3 class B players; blitz explains 64-81% of slow-game rank; Moxley 2012 found final moves were better than first moves.
agent_test: Do not cite Calderwood 1988 as proof of keep-first.

claim: Take-the-first in sport has mixed support: Johnson and Raab (handball) and Hepler and Feltz (N=72, heuristic used on 70% of trials, earlier options better) support the order effect, but the consistency and confidence claims failed in the replication, and the intuitive-to-analytical continuum evidence is inconsistent.
agent_test: Measure first, second, third generated option quality per item in the agent and check whether quality falls with order.

claim: Army planning variant of RPD (one base course of action, wargame it, drop comparison of three COAs) was estimated at least 30% faster by participants and about 20% faster in a Swedish study, with plans judged somewhat bolder. Evidence is by the model's developers and self-estimated.
agent_test: Compare single-COA plus pre-mortem versus three-COA comparison on a planning set at equal tokens, scored by a blind rater.

claim: An RPD-style prompt raised LLM triage accuracy from 63.3% to 67.6% (OR 2.26) over 10 ChatGPT models, 45 vignettes, 13,500 assessments (re-checked in the abstract and PMC text). The data-frame prompt gave 66.7%, so the gain is not specific to RPD.
agent_test: Run an RPD prompt, a different structured prompt and a length-matched control at equal tokens.

claim: The RPD prompt gain came from self-care cases (13.4% to 29.8%), helped reasoning models more (OR 2.15), vanished for GPT-5.2 (Instant 57.8 vs 56.4; Thinking 52.0 vs 53.1), raised accuracy in 18 of 45 cases but lowered it in 13, and did not make answers more stable (Fleiss kappa 0.766 to 0.717). Gap search (full text): the GPT-5.2 miss is a floor effect, self-care accuracy 0 to 3.1% under all prompts, while GPT-5.1 gained (Instant 5.4 to 33.1; Thinking 16.9 to 36.2). The paper has no length-matched neutral prompt, and the two NDM prompts scored almost the same (67.6 vs 66.7).
agent_test: Replicate on a second task and a non-OpenAI model family.

claim: In machines a fast first pass equals or beats slow reasoning on pattern-like tasks: CoT cost 23.1 points in implicit statistical learning (GPT-4o 87.5 to 64.4; the 36.3-point figure compares o1-preview 57.7 with GPT-4o direct 94.0 on a subset), CoT gave about no gain on commonsense, and NoThinking beat Thinking at low budgets (AMC23 at 700 tokens 51.3 vs 28.9).
schema_part: S1 gate: fast mode when pattern-like; O: parallel first tries plus selector
agent_test: Run N fast tries plus a selector against one long chain at matched tokens across pattern and symbolic tasks.
audit_note: Numbers all match (87.5->64.4 = 23.1; 36.3 is o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o direct 94.0 on 440-problem subset; AMC23 700 tokens 51.3 vs 28.9; Sprague: commonsense nearly no CoT gain). The NoThinking result is on math/proof/code tasks, not pattern-like tasks, so the 'pattern-like' framing is the note's.

claim: Fast no-think tries beat thinking at low token budgets even at pass@1, but at higher budgets thinking wins pass@1 and the fast-try advantage needs many samples plus a verifier or confidence-based selector (Ma et al.); on symbolic multi-step tasks CoT beats direct answering and tool-augmented solvers beat CoT (Sprague et al.).
agent_test: Hold budget fixed and vary whether a verifier is available.
audit_note: Ma et al. show NoThinking beats Thinking at pass@1 in the low-budget regime with no selector at all (Thinking wins pass@1 only at higher budgets, and on LiveCodeBench throughout), so the advantage does not wholly 'depend on' a selector; selectors/verifiers matter for turning pass@k into accuracy at matched latency. Sprague part is supported. Sources are two papers each listed twice.
claim_before_audit: The advantage of fast first tries depends on a selector or verifier. Without one thinking wins at higher budgets, and on symbolic multi-step tasks CoT and tools win.

claim: A recognition-only network can reach expert play without search (270M transformer: puzzles 95.4%, Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots), but it needs 15.3B labelled action values, and search still helps other systems (AlphaZero policy-only 56.1 vs 95.6 with 400 MCTS).
schema_part: memory (a case library is the agent analogue)
agent_test: Estimate how large a case memory is needed before keep-first matches search on a task family.
audit_note: Numbers match Ruoss et al. Table 1 and dataset text (95.4%, Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, 15.3B action values, AlphaZero 56.1 vs 95.6); caveat that the action-value labels come from Stockfish, a search engine, so 'recognition-only' is amortized search.

claim: Learned look-ahead exists inside a policy network: a probe predicts the best move two turns ahead at 92% accuracy, so pattern recognition can carry implicit simulation.
agent_test: Probe whether the agent's first option already encodes downstream consequences.

claim: Models can be trained to choose when to think: Thinkless cuts long-chain use 50-90% at comparable accuracy; Dualformer fast mode 80% optimal vs 30% solution-only, auto mode 96.6% with 59.9% fewer steps (re-checked in abstract). Gap search: a prompt-only or training-free gate now has tests. A draft-agreement gate (DART) matched or beat always-think on 13 of 14 pairs with 32 to 73% fewer thinking tokens, while a self-asked 'does this need thinking' gate did not beat always-think. No paper compares it head to head with Thinkless.
schema_part: S1 gate (learned or agreement-based); self-report gate is weak
agent_test: Build a prompt-only typicality gate and compare with an always-think baseline at equal tokens.
audit_note: Thinkless 50-90%, Dualformer 80 vs 30, 96.6 with 59.9% fewer steps, and DART 13 of 14 pairs with 32-73% fewer thinking tokens all verified in the papers (the miss is Qwen3-8B OlympiadBench, -1.7); the 'no head-to-head with Thinkless' statement is a search-gap remark that cannot be verified from sources.

claim: Fast rule layer plus slow LLM layer improved real-time play (DPT-Agent best on both maps, 68 valid human trials); the talker-reasoner paper reports no numbers.
schema_part: S: fast layer plus slow reviewer
agent_test: Only relevant to a single-agent text task if latency matters.

claim: GPT-3 gave the intuitive wrong answer on all 3 CRT items and human-like answers on 12 of 12 vignettes, so a first model answer can be a classic intuitive error.
schema_part: G (first answer may be intuitive error)
agent_test: Check first-answer error rate on CRT-like items for current models.

claim: In wargames LLM teams escalate and cannot be steered by persona: all five models escalated (GPT-3.5 10.15 to 26.02 in the paper's text), and 214 experts differed from LLM players on about half of the actions; pacifist vs aggressive persona made no significant difference.
schema_part: G: red-team check on first plan
agent_test: Score first-option aggressiveness against expert panel baselines.
audit_note: Supported by Lamparth (214 experts, agreement on about half of 21 actions, no significant persona effect) and Rivera (all five models show forms of escalation; GPT-3.5 10.15 to 26.02); caveats: Rivera says most escalation-score changes are not statistically significant, and the two studies use different setups (human-vs-LLM teams vs LLM nation agents).

claim: No study found tests an LLM on Klein's fireground paradigm, scores model first options against expert commanders, or measures how often a model's first option is workable on RPD-type cases. The search was limited by quota and 429 errors. Gap search (2026-11-01, limited by search quota): still no direct study. Closest are first-attempt plan validity rates on one validated domain, 8.8% to 97.8% across models (PlanBench, Blocksworld, n=600).
agent_test: This is the direct test to build.

claim: Model first-attempt plan validity varies from 8.8% (GPT-4o-mini) to 97.8% (o1-preview) on 600 zero-shot Blocksworld instances; GPT-4 first-plan validity was 40/100 in a separate test. So the 'first option is workable' rate must be measured per model and task, and cannot be assumed.
schema_part: S1 gate input: measured first-option rate
agent_test: Measure first-option workable rate on 100 held-out planning cases per model before enabling keep-first.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A same-model check (re-read, self-critique, mental simulation by the same model) with no external signal does not protect a first answer: GPT-4 self-critique approved 38 of 45 invalid plans, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 after one round, and GPT-4 GSM8K fell from 95.5 to 89.0 over two rounds. An external sound verifier raised GPT-4 plan validity from 40% to 88%.
schema_part: O: verify / select (needs an external check)
agent_test: At equal tokens compare keep-first+same-model-check vs keep-first+tool-check vs keep-first alone.
audit_note: All numbers match Huang et al. Table 3 and Valmeekam et al. (38 of 45 invalid plans passed, 40/100 to 88/100 with VAL plus backprompting); note the 88% includes backprompting iterations and Blocksworld only.

claim: A training-free typicality gate works on open-answer math and code: keep the answer when two cheap drafts agree, think otherwise (DART: 13 of 14 pairs matched or beat always-think, thinking tokens down 32 to 73%). The gate is weakest when drafts agree on a wrong answer (36 of 59 errors) and invalid on multiple choice.
agent_test: Port draft agreement to planning cases where answers are free text and agreement must be judged semantically.

claim: Asking the model whether a case needs thinking is an unreliable gate: MC-Binary and MC-Conf saved 4 and 24% tokens but fell to 10.4 and 8.5% on HumanEval and 54.9% on OlympiadBench (MC-Conf), and Self-Select in ranking stayed well under ideal routing.
schema_part: S1 gate: do not use self-report alone
agent_test: Compare self-report gate vs agreement gate vs retrieval-similarity gate at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match DART Table 2 and Think When Needed (Self-Select well under Ideal); slip: the 4% and 24% token savings are on MATH-500 where accuracy held, the HumanEval collapse (10.4, 8.5) comes with -7% and 44% savings, so the sentence merges columns.

claim: No single switching strategy wins across scales: prompt-based leads at 9B and 1.1T, speculative try-fast-then-escalate leads at 20B and 671B, all equal at 2B (HRBench, 527 runs); speculative gains most on code, at higher token cost.
agent_test: Choose keep-first gate by model size; do not copy a gate tuned for one scale.

claim: Task complexity moderates keep-first in LLMs: on easy items the first solution is usually enough (in over 92% of cases the first round already holds the correct answer, and o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 2+3) and later rounds add little; on hard puzzles models fixate on early wrong attempts, accuracy collapses, and even supplying the explicit algorithm did not help in the tested puzzles.
agent_test: Check that first-answer accuracy falls with problem size on the agent's own tasks.
audit_note: Numbers verified (1,953% more tokens on 2+3; over 92% of cases first round already correct, under 60% of tokens), but 'nothing helps' on hard puzzles goes beyond Shojaee et al., who show accuracy collapse at high complexity and no gain from giving the explicit algorithm, not that no intervention helps.
claim_before_audit: Task complexity moderates keep-first in LLMs: on easy items the first solution is usually enough (over 92% of correct responses had the correct answer in the first round; o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens on 2+3) and later rounds add little; on hard puzzles models fixate on early wrong attempts and nothing helps.

claim: Option order is a weak and unstable cue in LLMs: models favour the first-listed option when options are good and the last when they are poor (GPT-4o-mini first-choice 98% Ideal vs 21% Harsh), and reordering multiple-choice options moves accuracy by 13 to 75%. No study measures quality by generation order, and reasoning models were not tested.
schema_part: G: do not trust list position; shuffle when selecting
agent_test: Generate 5 options in one pass, score each with a validator, and plot score against generation index for a reasoning and a non-reasoning model.
audit_note: Numbers match (GPT-4o-mini 98% Ideal vs 21% Harsh first-listed; 13-75% gap in Pezeshkpour); the primacy-when-good, recency-when-poor pattern differs by model (Claude 3 Haiku already prefers the later option at Fair), and the 'no study' / 'reasoning models not tested' statements are search-gap remarks not checkable here.

claim: Stopping at the first finished chain is competitive on verifiable tasks: the shortest chain beat a random chain by up to 18.8 points and the longest by up to 34.5; short-1@k matched majority voting with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens. Agreement-based stopping cut samples up to 7.9 times with under 0.1% accuracy loss.
schema_part: Generate-test: stop early on agreement or first finish
agent_test: Equal-token test of first-finished vs compare-N on planning cases.
audit_note: Numbers match (18.8, 34.5, up to 40% fewer thinking tokens in low-compute settings; Adaptive-Consistency up to 7.9x with average accuracy drop under 0.1%); slips: the 0.1% is an average over datasets, and short-1@k matches majority voting only in low-compute settings.

claim: Recognition by trained pattern memory needs very large labelled data: in chess the policy network's accuracy rose with dataset size at every model size and large models overfit at 10K games; the strong model used 15.3B action values. No text-case-retrieval study gives a case count at which pattern recall replaces search.
agent_test: Vary the number of stored cases (10, 100, 1000) and plot keep-first accuracy.

claim: Gaps 7, 8 and 9 are unanswered by the gap search: no LLM token-cap blunder study, no blind-scored comparison of the Army single-COA method against three-COA comparison, and no test of whether keep-first weakens an adversary best-reply search. The search was blocked by quota and 429 errors, so this is a limit of the search.
agent_test: Run the three tests directly: token-capped agent on blunder tasks, blind-scored planning outcomes, red-team best-reply with and without keep-first.
